name: Transition Planning
title: Transition Planning
answer: Transition planning prepares students with disabilities for life after high school, including further education, work and independent living, and federal regulations require it in the IEP that will be in effect when a student turns 16. AI can help a team gather information about careers, training programs and support services, but the student's own goals and interests must drive the plan. It matters because the plan shapes what a student does after leaving school, and the student's voice is what keeps it meaningful.

sections.body: Transition planning is the part of a student's special education program that looks beyond high school to further education, work and independent living. The problem it solves is that planning for adult life can otherwise default to whatever options the adults in the room happen to know about, rather than what the student actually wants. AI can widen that view by helping a team gather information about careers, training programs and support services that match a student's interests and strengths. The student then explores those options and talks them over with the team and family. The plan is built around what the student wants, not around what the tool happened to suggest.
sections.heading: The idea

sections.body: The timing is set by regulation and by district choice. Transition planning must be in the IEP that will be in effect when a student turns 16, states may start earlier, and many districts begin at 14. In day to day work, a teacher can use an approved tool, with names removed, to research options that match a student's interests and strengths, and the student then explores those options and discusses them with the team and family. Students should lead their transition planning as much as possible, and some can use AI tools to research careers, practice interview questions or draft a letter to an employer, with support. These are real skills they will need after high school.
sections.heading: How it works in school

sections.body: The text offers no study, figure or evidence label for this idea. What it does give is a legal requirement, citing Individuals with Disabilities Education Act regulations, 34 C.F.R. § 300.320, which require transition planning in the IEP that will be in effect when a student turns 16, with states permitted to start earlier and many districts beginning at 14. Beyond that requirement, the idea as presented here rests on practice rather than research.
sections.heading: What the evidence says

sections.body: The limits in the text are about who stays in charge. A teacher using an approved tool should remove names before researching options, so student information is not fed into it. The team makes sure the student's voice, not the tool's suggestions, drives the plan, which means AI output is treated as material to consider rather than a decision already made. Students lead their planning as much as possible, and where they use AI to research careers, practice interview questions or draft a letter to an employer, they do so with support. The choices about what the student will pursue after high school stay with the student, the family and the team.
